title: In 1518, people danced until they collapsed

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: In 1518, a whole city watched people dance until they collapsed.
beats.visual: Hondius 'Dancing Mania' engraving, figures animated in a jerky loop

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: Strasbourg, July 1518: a woman, Frau Troffea, began dancing alone in the street.
beats.visual: Sketch map: Strasbourg on the Rhine; one dancing silhouette on a cobbled street

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: Days, by later accounts. About thirty more joined her. But there was a problem. Nobody could stop it.
beats.visual: Day counter reaches 6; more silhouettes join the dance

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: Doctors blamed overheated blood, so officials built a stage and hired musicians.
beats.visual: Two panels: doctor holding a blood drop; carpenters raising a stage, pipers and drummers

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: It made it worse. Reports say up to 400 danced. Some collapsed; later accounts claim deaths.
beats.visual: Crowd fills the frame; counter 'up to 400?'; figures slump to the ground

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: The council banned dancing. By September it faded. Historians still debate why.
beats.visual: Brant's 1518 dance-ban notice slides in; question mark over the city

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: A city that couldn't stop dancing. Follow History Sketches for one wild true story every day.
beats.visual: Last dancer freezes mid-step; History Sketches corner logo

description: In July 1518 a woman in Strasbourg began dancing in the street, and within weeks reports say up to 400 people had joined her. The city's cure, more music, made it worse. Narration: synthetic voices. Facts checked against two sources. #history #shorts #strangehistory #medieval
